p.src: Now the brocade-robed officer dragged the false Tang Monk out of the posthouse, and, surrounded on every side by the Imperial Guards, escorted him straight to the palace gate. There he said to the eunuch gatekeeper, “We have brought the Tang Monk here. Please report our arrival.” The eunuch hurried into court and reported to the benighted king just as he had been told, whereupon the monk was summoned inside. All the officials knelt below the steps in homage, but the false Tang Monk alone stood erect in the middle of the stairway and called aloud, “King of Bhikṣu, why have you summoned this poor monk?” The king smiled and said, “We have contracted an illness that has lingered long without healing. Fortunately, Our Royal Father-in-law has bestowed upon us a prescription. All the medicines are prepared, and only one ingredient for the medicinal catalyst is lacking. We have therefore specially invited you, Elder, to ask you for some of that catalyst. If it cures Our illness, We shall build a shrine for you, Elder, offer sacrifices in all four seasons, and preserve your worship as an everlasting institution of the realm.” The false Tang Monk said, “I am a man who has left the household and have come here alone. I do not know what your Majesty asked the Royal Father-in-law to use as the catalyst.” The benighted king replied, “We ask only for your heart and liver, Elder.” The false Tang Monk said, “To tell your Majesty the truth, I have several hearts. I do not know what color and kind you require.” The Royal Father-in-law pointed at him from the side and said, “Monk, it is your black heart we want.” The false Tang Monk said, “If that is so, bring me a knife at once and cut open my chest and belly. If there is a black heart inside, I shall respectfully obey your command.” The benighted king thanked him delightedly and immediately ordered an attendant of the imperial carriage to fetch a short ox-ear knife and hand it to the false monk. Taking the knife in hand, the false monk loosened his clothes and thrust out his chest. He rubbed his belly with his left hand and held the knife in his right; then, with a ripping sound, he sliced open his belly, and from within there came tumbling out a whole heap of hearts. The civil officials turned pale with fright, and the military commanders went numb all over. Seeing this from the hall, the Royal Father-in-law said, “This is a monk of many hearts.” The false monk picked through those blood-dripping hearts one by one and displayed them to everyone. There were red hearts, white hearts, yellow hearts, miserly and greedy hearts, hearts set on profit and fame, jealous hearts, calculating hearts, contentious hearts, ambitious hearts, arrogant hearts, murderous hearts, cruel and venomous hearts, fearful hearts, cautious hearts, perverse and deluded hearts, obscure and benighted hearts, and every other kind of wicked heart—but not a single black heart among them. The benighted king was so terrified that he sat dazed and rigid, unable to speak. Trembling, he ordered, “Put them away! Put them away!” The false Tang Monk could endure no more. He withdrew his magical hearts, revealed his true form, and said to the benighted king, “Your Majesty has no discernment whatsoever. We monks possess only good hearts. It is this Royal Father-in-law of yours who has a black heart, just right for your medicinal catalyst. If you do not believe me, wait while I take his out and show it to you.”

p.src: The fiend fought bitterly with Pilgrim for more than twenty rounds, but his coiling-dragon staff could not withstand the Gold-Banded Cudgel. Feinting once with his staff, he transformed himself into a streak of cold light and descended into the inner palace. There he carried the demon queen who had been presented as tribute out through the palace gate; together they turned into cold light and vanished without a trace.

p.src: The Great Sage lowered his cloud and came down before the palace hall. He said to the assembled officials, “What an excellent Royal Father-in-law you had!” All the officials bowed together and thanked the divine monk. Pilgrim said, “Never mind bowing for now. Go and see where that benighted ruler of yours is.” The officials replied, “When our lord saw the battle, he hid himself in terror. We do not know which palace he fled to.” Pilgrim immediately ordered them, “Find him quickly, lest the beautiful queen carry him off.” Hearing this, the officials searched both the inner and outer courts. Together with Pilgrim, they first hurried to the beautiful queen’s palace, but there was no trace of anyone; even the beautiful queen had completely disappeared. The principal queen, the ladies of the eastern and western palaces and the six courts—in short, all the consorts—came to bow and thank the Great Sage. The Great Sage said, “Please rise for now. It is not yet time to thank me. Go and find your sovereign first.” Before long, four or five eunuchs appeared, supporting the benighted king as they came from behind the Hall of Personal Cultivation. The assembled ministers prostrated themselves and reported with one voice, “Our lord! Our lord! By good fortune the divine monk came here and distinguished truth from falsehood. That Royal Father-in-law was an evil fiend, and the beautiful queen too has disappeared.” On hearing this, the king invited Pilgrim out of the inner palace and into the main audience hall. After bowing his thanks, he said, “Elder, when you came this morning you had such a handsome and imposing appearance. Why have you changed your looks now?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “To tell your Majesty the truth, the one who came this morning was my master, Tripitaka, the imperial brother of the Tang emperor. I am his disciple Sun Wukong. He also has two other disciples, Zhu Wuneng and Sha Wujing, who are now at the Golden Pavilion Posthouse. When I learned that you had believed a fiend’s words and meant to take my master’s heart and liver for a medicinal catalyst, I, Old Sun, assumed my master’s appearance and came here expressly to subdue the demon.” When the king heard this, he immediately issued a decree ordering the grand minister in attendance to hurry to the posthouse and invite the master and his disciples to court.

p.src: When Tripitaka heard that Pilgrim had revealed his true form and was subduing the fiend in the sky, he was so terrified that his soul nearly fled his body. Fortunately, Bajie and Sha Monk were there to protect him, though his face was still covered with a layer of foul-smelling mud. As he brooded unhappily, he suddenly heard someone call, “Master, we are grand ministers sent by the King of Bhikṣu. We have come expressly to invite you to court so that he may thank you for your grace.” Bajie laughed and said, “Master, don’t be afraid, don’t be afraid. They have not come to take your heart again. I expect Elder Brother has won, and they are inviting you so they can offer their thanks.” Tripitaka said, “They may be inviting me because he has won, but with this stinking face of mine, how can I meet anyone?” Bajie replied, “It cannot be helped. Let us first go and see Elder Brother; he will have some explanation for it.” The Elder truly had no other recourse, so he followed Bajie and Sha Monk, who carried the luggage and led the horse, and together they went out into the posthouse courtyard. When the grand minister saw them, he cried in fear, “Good heavens! These all look like monstrous, fiendish creatures!” Sha Monk said, “My lord, do not take offense at our ugliness. These are the bodies with which we were born. As for my master, once he has seen my elder brother, he will become handsome again.”

p.src: The three of them came to court with the others and, without waiting to be summoned, went straight to the foot of the throne. Seeing them, Monkey turned and descended from the dais. He went to meet them, tore the clay mask from his master's face, breathed an immortal breath upon him, and cried, “Change!” Tripitaka instantly regained his true form and felt more refreshed and vigorous than ever. The king descended from the throne to welcome him in person, addressing him as “Venerable Master and Buddha.” The master and disciples tethered the horse, then all came up into the hall to meet the king. Monkey said, “Does Your Majesty know where that monster came from? Let old Monkey go and capture the whole lot for you, rooting out any future trouble.” All the ladies of the three palaces and six courts—the consorts and imperial concubines—were behind the jadeite screen. When they heard Monkey speak of ending the future threat, they disregarded the propriety separating men and women and came out together to bow and plead: “We earnestly beg the holy monk and venerable Buddha to display his mighty powers, tear the evil out by the roots, and utterly destroy him. That would be an immeasurable kindness, and we shall certainly repay it richly.” Monkey hurriedly returned their bows and merely asked the king to tell him where the monster lived. The king replied shamefacedly, “When he came three years ago, We did ask him. He said that not far from the city, seventy li to the south, there was a place called Qinghua Manor on Willow-Grove Slope. The Royal Father-in-law, he said, was elderly and had no son, but his second wife had borne him a daughter, just sixteen and not yet betrothed, whom he wished to present to Us. Because We loved the girl, We accepted her and made her Our favored consort in the palace. Unexpectedly, We fell ill, and repeated medicines from the imperial physicians proved useless. He said, ‘I have an immortal prescription. It requires only a child's heart, decocted as the medicinal vehicle.’ In Our unworthiness, We rashly believed his words and had children selected from among the people, appointing noon today as the time to cut them open and take their hearts. We never expected the holy monk to descend among us just as all the children's cages mysteriously vanished. He then said that the holy monk had cultivated the Way through ten incarnations and had never spent his primal yang, so that his heart would be ten thousand times better than the hearts of children. In a moment of delusion We committed this offense, not knowing that the holy monk had seen through the fiend. We dare hope that you will exercise your great powers and remove this future threat; We shall reward you with the wealth of Our entire kingdom.” Monkey laughed. “To tell you the truth, it was at my compassionate master's bidding that I hid the children from the cages. Say no more about rewarding me with riches. Capturing the monster will itself count toward my religious merit.” He called, “Bajie, come with me.” Bajie replied, “I shall obey you, Brother. But my belly is empty, and I cannot put forth much strength.” The king immediately issued an order for the Court of Imperial Entertainments to prepare a vegetarian meal without delay. Before long, the meal arrived. Bajie ate his fill, roused his spirits, and followed Monkey as he mounted the clouds. The king, his queens and consorts, and all the civil and military officials were so astonished that they bowed one after another toward the sky, saying, “True immortals and true Buddhas have descended to the mortal world!”

They saw only a clear stream enclosed by two banks, with countless willows growing along them, and had no idea where Qinghua Manor might be. Just as the verse says:

p.src: Unable to find the place, the Great Sage Sun formed a hand seal, recited the true-word “Om,” and summoned the local earth god. Trembling, the god approached, knelt, and cried, “Great Sage, the earth god of Willow-Grove Slope kowtows before you.” Monkey said, “Do not be afraid. I will not beat you. I ask you: where on Willow-Grove Slope is the place called Qinghua Manor?” The earth god replied, “There is a Qinghua Cave here, but there has never been a Qinghua Manor. I understand now. Has the Great Sage perhaps come from the Kingdom of Bhiksu?” Monkey said, “Exactly, exactly. The king of Bhiksu was deceived by a fiend. When old Monkey arrived there, I recognized it as a monster and drove it back in battle, whereupon it transformed into a cold beam of light and vanished to parts unknown. When I questioned the king of Bhiksu, he said that three years ago, when the fiend presented him with a beauty, he asked where it came from, and the monster claimed to live at Qinghua Manor on Willow-Grove Slope, seventy li south of the city. I have just searched my way here, but I see only the wooded slope and no Qinghua Manor. That is why I asked you.” The earth god kowtowed and said, “I beg the Great Sage to forgive my offense. The king of Bhiksu is also the sovereign of this land, so it was my duty to keep watch over the matter. But the fiend possesses such awesome might and powerful magic that if I revealed anything about him, he would come and torment me. Thus I have been unable to expose him. Now that the Great Sage has come, go to the south bank, to the roots of the nine-forked poplar. Circle three times to the left and three times to the right, slap the tree with both hands together, and call ‘Open the door!’ three times. The Qinghua Cave residence will then appear.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Great Sage dismissed the earth god, then crossed the stream with Bajie and searched for that poplar. Sure enough, there were nine forked branches, all growing from a single root. Monkey instructed Bajie, “Stand well back. I shall call the door open and seek out the monster. When I drive him outside, you are to support me.” Obeying the order, Bajie took up his position about half a li from the tree. Following the earth god's instructions, the Great Sage circled the roots three times to the left and three times to the right, slapped the tree with both hands, and cried, “Open the door! Open the door!” In an instant there came a loud report, and with a rumble two doors swung open; not a trace of the tree remained. Within was a radiant glow of rosy light, but not a sign of human habitation. Relying on his divine prowess, Monkey charged inside, where he found a truly splendid place:

p.src: Monkey hurried forward and looked closely. On a stone screen he saw four large characters: “Qinghua Immortal Residence.” Unable to restrain himself, he leaped over the stone screen and looked beyond it. There he saw the old monster embracing a beautiful woman. Panting heavily, they were discussing the affairs of the Kingdom of Bhiksu and saying together, “What a fine opportunity it was! After three years the business was to be completed today, only to be ruined by that monkey!” Monkey rushed up, drew his staff, and cried, “You pack of hairy beasts! What do you mean by a ‘fine opportunity’? Taste my staff!” The old monster dropped the beauty, swung up his coiling-dragon crutch, and hastily parried the blow. The two fought before the cave, and this fierce battle was quite unlike the one before:

p.src: Bajie, meanwhile, was outside. Hearing the uproar within made him itch unbearably to join the fight. He drew his rake, raked down the nine-forked poplar, and struck it several times. Fresh blood gushed from it, and it seemed to whimper aloud. He cried, “This tree has become a spirit too! This tree has become a spirit too!” Bajie raised his rake and was just about to strike again when he saw Monkey driving the monster outside. Without a word, the Fool rushed forward and brought down his rake. The old monster was already hard-pressed in his fight with Monkey. When he saw Bajie's rake descending, he grew even more alarmed. Defeated, he shook his body, transformed into a cold beam of light, and fled straight east. The two of them refused to let him escape and pursued him eastward.

p.src: Just as the cries of battle rang out, they heard cranes calling, and an auspicious radiance shimmered in the distance. Looking up, they saw that it was the Old Man of the Southern Pole, the Star of Longevity. The old immortal covered the cold gleam and called, “Great Sage, stay your hand! Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds, cease your pursuit! This old Daoist offers his respects.” Pilgrim returned the courtesy and said, “Brother Star of Longevity, what brings you here?” Eight Rules laughed. “That lump-headed old fellow has trapped the cold gleam. He must have caught the monster.” The Star of Longevity smiled apologetically. “He is here, he is here. I beg you both to spare his life.” Pilgrim said, “This old monster has nothing to do with you, brother. Why plead on his behalf?” The Star of Longevity laughed. “He is my mount. I never expected him to run away and come here to turn into a monster.” Pilgrim said, “If he belongs to you, brother, have him show us his true form.” Hearing this, the Star of Longevity released the cold gleam and shouted, “Wretched beast! Show your true form at once, and your death sentence shall be remitted.” The monster spun around and proved to be a white deer. The Star of Longevity picked up his staff and said, “The wretched beast even stole my staff.” The deer prostrated itself on the ground. Unable to speak, it merely kowtowed and shed tears. This was how he appeared:

p.src: Eight Rules roused his spirits and followed Pilgrim straight into the Immortal Residence of Pure Splendor, where he bellowed, “Catch the monster! Catch the monster!” The beauty was already trembling with fear and had no way to escape. Hearing the shouts grow thunderous, she slipped behind the stone screen, but there was no back door through which to flee. Eight Rules roared, “Where do you think you are going? You shameless seductress who deceives men—taste my rake!” The beauty had no weapon and could not meet him in battle. She twisted aside, changed into a cold gleam, and sped toward the outside. The Great Sage blocked the cold gleam and struck it with a resounding blow of his cudgel. The monster lost her footing and fell into the dust, revealing her true form: a white-faced vixen. The Fool could not restrain himself and brought his rake down upon her head. Alas, the thousand smiles of that beauty who could topple cities and kingdoms were transformed into a furry ball in the shape of a fox. Pilgrim cried, “Do not smash her to pieces. Keep the body intact to show that benighted king.”

p.src: Untroubled by the filth, the Fool grabbed the fox by the tail and dragged it along as he followed Pilgrim out through the gate. There they saw the old Star of Longevity stroking the deer’s head and scolding it: “You wretched beast! How could you desert your master, run away, and turn into a monster here? Had I not come, the Great Sage Sun would surely have beaten you to death.” Pilgrim sprang out and said, “What are you saying, brother?” The Star of Longevity replied, “I am admonishing the deer, merely admonishing the deer.” Eight Rules flung the dead fox down before the deer and said, “Is this your daughter?” The deer nodded and shook its head, stretched out its muzzle to sniff her several times, and bleated softly, as though loath to part from her. The Star of Longevity slapped it squarely on the head and said, “Wretched beast! You should be thankful merely to have escaped with your life. Why are you still sniffing her?” He removed the sash from his robe, fastened it around the deer’s neck, pulled the animal to its feet, and said, “Great Sage, let us meet again in the kingdom of Bhiksuland.” Pilgrim said, “Wait. We may as well sweep this whole place clean, lest monsters arise here again in years to come.”

p.src: Hearing this, Eight Rules raised his rake and hacked wildly at the willow trees. Pilgrim again recited the true formula of the syllable “Om,” summoned the local earth god as before, and ordered him: “Find some dry firewood and kindle a great blaze. We shall rid your district of this monstrous scourge and spare it further oppression.” The earth god turned away at once. With a soughing yin wind he marshaled his spirit soldiers, who brought frost grass, autumn-green grass, knotweed stalks, mountain-blossom grass, southernwood, dragon-bone wood, and reed and rush wood. All were parched remnants dried through from the previous year, and caught fire as readily as oil. Pilgrim called, “Eight Rules, there is no need to batter the trees. Just stuff all this into the cave, set it alight, and burn the place clean.” Once the fire was lit, the monsters’ Pure Splendor residence was indeed burned into a blazing pit.

p.src: Only then did they dismiss the earth god. Together with the Star of Longevity, they led the deer and dragged the fox back before the throne, saying to the king, “Here is your lovely queen. Would you care to dally with her now?” The king trembled with terror. Then they saw the Great Sage Sun lead in the Star of Longevity with the white deer in tow. The sight so frightened the sovereign, ministers, consorts, and queen that they all bowed down together. Pilgrim stepped forward, helped the king up, and said with a laugh, “Do not bow to me. This little deer is your royal father-in-law; you need only bow to him.” The king was overwhelmed with shame and could only say, “I thank the holy monks for saving the children of my entire realm. This is truly grace from Heaven.” He immediately issued an order for the Court of Imperial Entertainments to prepare a vegetarian banquet, opened the Eastern Pavilion, and invited the Old Man of the Southern Pole and the four pilgrims to dine while he offered thanks. Tripitaka paid his respects to the Star of Longevity, and Friar Sand likewise greeted him with due ceremony. They all asked, “Since the white deer belongs to the venerable Star of Longevity, how did it come here and cause such harm?” The Star of Longevity laughed. “Some time ago, the Sovereign Lord of the Eastern Florescence passed my humble mountain. I asked him to stay for a game of chess, and before we had finished, this wretched beast ran away. When my guest had gone, I searched but could not find him. I calculated on my fingers, learned that he had fled here, and came expressly to retrieve him, just as the Great Sage Sun was displaying his might. Had I truly arrived any later, this beast would have been finished.”

p.src: They then arranged the seating: the Star of Longevity occupied the place of honor, the elder monk sat next, the king sat facing them, and Pilgrim, Eight Rules, and Friar Sand took side seats. Two or three senior monks sat nearby to keep them company. The king then ordered the Imperial Music Office to begin playing. Holding a Purple Cloud cup, the king personally offered wine to each guest. Tripitaka alone did not drink. Eight Rules said to Pilgrim, “Brother, I shall leave the fruit to you, but you must let me enjoy the soup and rice.” The Fool paid no heed to what was fine or coarse. He piled everything together and ate every dish that came until nothing remained.

p.src: When the banquet was over, the Star of Longevity took his leave. The king again approached and knelt before him, begging for a method to dispel sickness and prolong life. The Star of Longevity laughed. “As I came in search of my deer, I brought no elixir with me. I might teach you a method of cultivating life, but your sinews are feeble and your spirit depleted, so you cannot restore the elixir within yourself. I have only three dates in my sleeve, which were served with tea for the Sovereign Lord of the Eastern Florescence. I did not eat them, so I shall give them to you now.” The king swallowed them and gradually felt his body grow light and his illness recede. His later longevity all had its origin in this. Seeing this, Eight Rules called, “Old Longevity, if you have fire dates, give me a few to eat.” The Star of Longevity said, “I did not bring any. Another day I shall send you several catties.” He then left the Eastern Pavilion, offered his thanks, shouted a command that brought the white deer to its feet, leapt onto its back, and departed upon the clouds. The king, consorts, and queen at court, and all the common people dwelling in the city, each burned incense and bowed in worship; of this no more need be said.

p.src: Tripitaka called out, “Disciples, pack up and bid farewell to the king.” But the king earnestly pressed them to stay and begged for instruction. Pilgrim said, “Your Majesty, henceforth indulge less in carnal desire and accumulate more hidden merit. In all things, make good what is lacking with what is abundant; that alone will suffice to dispel illness and prolong your life. That is the instruction I offer.” The king then brought out two trays of loose gold and pieces of silver and offered them as traveling expenses. The Tang monk firmly declined and would not accept so much as a penny. Having no other recourse, the king ordered the imperial equipage prepared and invited the Tang monk to sit upright in the phoenix palanquin and dragon carriage. The king and his consorts all helped push the wheels and turn the hubs as they escorted him out of the court. Throughout the six thoroughfares and three marketplaces, all the common people likewise set out cups of pure water and burned true incense in their censers, accompanying the travelers beyond the city walls.

p.src: Suddenly there came a rush of wind from midair, and on both sides of the road descended one thousand one hundred and eleven goose cages, from within which children could be heard crying. Concealed from sight were the city gods, earth gods, gods of the soil, divine officers, the Guardians of the Five Directions, the Duty Officers of the Four Watches, the Six Dings and Six Jias, the guardian deities of the faith, and all the others who had originally protected them. They called out together in loud voices: “Great Sage, by your earlier command we carried away the children and their goose cages. Now that we know your work is complete and you are setting forth, we have brought every one of them back.” The king, his consorts, and all his ministers and subjects once again bowed down together. Pilgrim looked up into the air and said, “You have all taken much trouble. Please return to your shrines; I shall have the people offer sacrifices in gratitude to you.” With a whistling and rustling, the chill wind rose once more and withdrew.

p.src: Pilgrim called for the families in the city to come and claim their children. Word spread at once, and every family came to recognize its own child in the cages. Overjoyed, they lifted the children out, calling them “dear brother” and “my darling,” some leaping, others laughing. They all cried, “Hold on to the venerable masters from the Tang court and bring them to our homes, so that we may thank them for saving our children!” Old and young, men and women alike, none of them feared the disciples’ ugly appearances. They hoisted Zhu Bajie aloft, shouldered Friar Sand, raised the Great Sage Sun above their heads, and bore up Tang Tripitaka; then, leading the horse and carrying the luggage, they surged back into the city in one great throng. Even the king was unable to restrain them. One household laid on a banquet, and another spread a feast. Those who could not invite them made monks’ caps, monks’ shoes, short robes, or cloth socks instead, and came bearing clothes of every size, both inner and outer garments, as farewell gifts. Thus they remained there for nearly a month before they were finally able to leave the city. Portraits of them were also handed down, and memorial tablets were erected before which the people bowed, burned incense, and made offerings. And so it truly was:
